title: Paula and Eustochium
hook: a Roman widow and her daughter who studied Hebrew and worked with Jerome

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jerome's line, ignorance of scripture is ignorance of Christ. Your line was know the book, know him. Which line from the Gospel page stayed with you? Day seven hundred forty-three.

Jerome wrote a long letter about a mother after she died, and one scene in it is hard to read. A small boy on the shore stretches out his hands toward her, and his sister silently begs her to wait. The ship is ready to sail east. The mother is Paula, a wealthy Roman widow. Beside her on deck is her daughter Eustochium. Jerome says Paula lifted her eyes to heaven and didn't look back at the shore. Jerome doesn't pretend it was easy; he says it tore at her. She was leaving a whole life behind for Bethlehem.
screen: `A BOY ON THE SHORE.` → `A SHIP READY TO SAIL.` → `PAULA SAILS FOR BETHLEHEM.`

segments.voice: First, who they were. Paula came from the Roman nobility. Eustochium was one of her daughters. Both had studied scripture in Rome in a circle of women Jerome taught, before any of them left. Second, the language. In Bethlehem, Jerome says, Paula set out to learn Hebrew, so she could sing the psalms in the language they were written in. And he says she managed it, and Eustochium too. These weren't patrons who simply paid for a scholar's work. They were students of the text, reading it in the original alongside him. Third, the questions. Jerome says Paula made him read through the scriptures with her. And when he hit a passage he couldn't explain, and honestly said so, she wouldn't let it go. She'd press him with fresh questions until he told her which meaning he thought most likely. A student like that makes a teacher better. Fourth, what they built. In Bethlehem, Paula founded communities for women living a life of prayer, and a place to welcome pilgrims. Jerome dedicated works to them, and after Paula died he wrote her long epitaph as a letter to Eustochium. He says she died with verses of the psalms on her lips, the psalms she had worked so hard to learn. So Jerome's Bible didn't come from a scholar working alone. In Bethlehem he worked alongside two women of the book who wouldn't stop asking.
screen: `A ROMAN WIDOW AND HER DAUGHTER.` · `THEY LEARNED HEBREW.` · `SHE WOULDN'T LET A QUESTION GO.` · `A TEAM IN BETHLEHEM.` · then, large: `WOMEN OF THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a woman scholar. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a woman who knows something deeply and wouldn't let you read it carelessly. Someone who pressed you with a question you couldn't answer yet, or sat with you over a hard page. Remember one moment with her. Hold it for a while. Then decide how you'll thank her: a message, a note, a call. If she's gone, or out of reach, you can simply say her name. If you pray, you can thank God for her. The bell holds the time.
Paula. The Roman widow who left everything for Bethlehem, learned Hebrew, and pressed Jerome with questions about the scriptures. Today's word.
Your line: women of the book. Today, send the thank-you you just planned. One sentence is enough. Day seven hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Paula and Saint Eustochium as saints, and Jerome's letters to and about them are among the main sources for their lives.

notes: All of Letter 108 is paraphrased; section numbers are approximate and should be checked.
The harbor scene (108.6): Toxotius stretching out his hands, Rufina pleading silently, Paula lifting her eyes to heaven. Children not named in the voice.
Paula and Eustochium learning Hebrew to sing the psalms (108.26): confirm that Jerome says Eustochium did too.
Paula pressing Jerome with questions (108.26): confirm the paraphrase.
'A circle of women Jerome taught' in Rome (the Aventine circle around Marcella): confirm.
'Communities for women ... and a place to welcome pilgrims': Paula founded monasteries and a hospice in Bethlehem; confirm.
Dying with psalm verses on her lips (108.28): confirm.
howItsDone: Paula (Jan 26) and Eustochium (Sept 28) are honored as saints; confirm.
